tier_reason: First-party numbers from the README. The benchmark code is public (tests/integration/speed/latency/client.js, tests/integration/speed/sync) and the hardware and runtime are stated (i7-6700HQ, Node v8.0.0). But Kafka is never run by this benchmark: its figures are quoted from LinkedIn's separate 3-machine 2014 benchmark, so the result falls short of A.

corrections.license: MIT (declared in the README's License section, 'MIT License © Pedram Emrouznejad', and in package.json as 'pemrouz.mit-license.org'; no LICENSE file, so GitHub reports no SPDX id)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Round-trip latency over 10,000 messages: median 0.06 ms vs Kafka's reported 2 ms (~33x), 99th percentile 0.3 ms vs 3 ms (~10x), 99.9th percentile 1.86 ms vs 14 ms (~7.5x) (ratios derived from page data). ZeroMQ's reported average of 0.06 ms is about the same as fero's 0.07 ms mean. Throughput at 100-byte messages is ~72 MB/s (755,419 records/s) vs ~75 MB/s (795,064 records/s) for LinkedIn's Kafka, roughly on par. The author reads ~10 vs ~5 MB/s at 10 bytes and ~161 vs ~80 MB/s at 1000 bytes off LinkedIn's graph. On 10-byte vs 3-byte writes, fero does 1,075,657 records/s vs Redis's best-case 552,028.75 records/s (~1.9x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: This is an indirect, apples-to-oranges comparison. Fero measures round-trip latency over localhost on one laptop against a single node. The Kafka figures are LinkedIn's end-to-end, producer-to-consumer numbers from a separately run 3-machine benchmark with replication (confirmed on engineering.linkedin.com). The 10-byte and 1000-byte Kafka throughput numbers are the author's readings of LinkedIn's graph. The Redis numbers were taken on a different (Xeon) machine. MIT is declared only in the README and package.json; there is no LICENSE file. The project has been unmaintained since April 2018.

notes: The README numbers and the LinkedIn figures it cites (2/3/14 ms, 795,064 records/s at 75.8 MB/s) both check out. The main fix is the license: MIT is declared in the README, so the entry is copyable, not reference-only. The metadata is otherwise accurate: 176 stars, last commit 2018-04-22, not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: A Harper-affiliated first-party benchmark. The harness is public (harness/, baseline/, harper/, scripts/campaign-w*.sh) and the Kafka settings are stated. The hardware is given only as 'Apple Silicon Mac (M-series)' running an OrbStack VM with 24 GB and 8 vCPU, with no exact CPU model, so it is not A. It is not independent or peer-reviewed, so it is not B.

corrections.hardware: A single virtualized environment on an Apple Silicon Mac (M-series; exact chip not stated) under OrbStack, with 24 GB RAM, 8 vCPU and virtualized storage. Each of the 3 Harper nodes is capped at 2.6 vCPU and 4.6 GB.
corrections.license: The Harper Pro image under test is Elastic-2.0 (source-available, non-OSI; source at github.com/HarperFast/harper-pro). The open-source Harper core (github.com/HarperFast/harper) is Apache-2.0, and the benchmark harness is Apache-2.0.
corrections.caveats: The author discloses Harper affiliation and invites Kafka experts to audit the setup. Everything runs on a single Apple Silicon laptop VM, which the README calls 'the largest known limitation'. The README says W4 above ~1,000 events/s is 'a laptop-VM artifact, not a system limit' and does not reflect Kafka's real throughput ceiling. No exact CPU model is given. The ~100x (W1) and ~40x (W4) figures compare whole stacks (PG+Debezium+Kafka, Kafka+Redis), not bare Kafka. Harper's source is public: the core is Apache-2.0 and Harper Pro is source-available under Elastic-2.0.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches the README table exactly, including the p50 figures and Kafka's W3 point-lookup win. The record wrongly says Harper's source is not public: HarperFast/harper (JavaScript, Apache-2.0, 90 stars, active) and HarperFast/harper-pro (Elastic License) both exist. The orchestrator may want repo_url set to https://github.com/HarperFast/harper, since that field is not correctable here. The benchmark_url on blob/master 302-redirects to main, the only branch.

tier_reason: First-party README claim of 89 ms vs Redis's 5 s. The Redis-side benchmark code is in the repo (redisBenchmark.cpp) and the uWS side points to deepstream.io-benchmarks, but no hardware, compiler or flags are given, and the >50x ratio with unstated flags is capped at C.

corrections.workload: Broadcast-coalescing pub/sub prototype on µWebSockets, run against the deepstream.io event benchmark, compared with Redis pub/sub on the same problem size. The in-repo redisBenchmark.cpp (hiredis async plus libuv, localhost) opens 9,000 subscribers and 1,000 publishers; each publisher sends a 1-byte message to one channel, for 9M deliveries per round, and it times the round. Message count and size come from that file; the README text does not state them.
corrections.caveats: No hardware, compiler or flags are given for either side. Only the Redis-side harness is in the repo; the uWS side relies on the external deepstream.io-benchmarks client. The ratios (>50x vs Redis, >3000x vs Socket.IO) are first-party and unreproduced. All commits are authored by Alex Hultman (uWebSockets author, Nov 2016), so this is a non-fork re-upload of his repo; the likely original, alexhultman/High-performance-pub-sub, returns 404. The Zlib license has no patent grant.

notes: The README numbers match the record (89 ms vs 5 s for Redis, 4.5 min for Socket.IO). The metadata checks out: Zlib (LICENSE text confirmed), 14 stars, last commit 2016-11-25, not archived, not a GitHub fork. The workload is corrected because redisBenchmark.cpp does state the problem size.
